summary: This case study details a security audit and architectural hardening across a fleet of 40+ Next.js SaaS applications proxying requests to generative AI providers. It shares practical, actionable insights on in-memory serverless rate limiting, atomic SQL credit deduction, and fleet-wide code audit pitfalls.
strengths: High practical relevance for engineering teams running AI wrapper SaaS applications susceptible to cost-draining abuse.
Clear, battle-tested code patterns for cheap in-memory IP throttling, dual-bucket anonymous/authenticated routing, and atomic credit deductions via SQL WHERE clauses.
Insightful documentation of fleet audit pitfalls, including false negatives caused by naming convention drift and phantom security comments in lieu of actual code.
Well-structured defense-in-depth model that orders checks strictly from cheapest (in-memory lookup) to most expensive (vendor API call).
weaknesses: No public repository is provided to reproduce the fleet scanner tooling or inspect the template implementation end-to-end.
In-memory fixed-window rate limiting on serverless platforms lacks true burst coordination under horizontal auto-scaling compared to distributed token-bucket stores.
The client IP extraction function relies naively on `x-forwarded-for` without discussing spoofing risks when applications sit behind multi-hop proxies or misconfigured CDNs.
suggestions: Add guidance on validating trusted reverse proxy hops when reading `x-forwarded-for` to prevent IP spoofing header attacks.
Provide benchmark or telemetry data comparing error rates and vendor spend before and after deploying the template-level fix across the fleet.

claims.text: The Map is module-level, not request-level. This means it persists across requests within a single serverless instance lifetime. On Vercel, instances are reused for multiple requests until they go cold.
For perfect cross-instance consistency, the upgrade path is @upstash/ratelimit with Redis.
The WHERE credits >= amount clause ensures the update only succeeds if the user has sufficient balance at the moment the row is locked for update.
claims.source: PostgreSQL and standard SQL concurrency semantics (UPDATE row-level locking)
